clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic LCAT variants; the enzyme esterifies free cholesterol on HDL, so its loss impairs reverse cholesterol transport and cholesterol esterification in plasma.
Two overlapping phenotypes exist: complete deficiency (classic familial LCAT deficiency) and partial deficiency (fish-eye disease), distinguished by whether alpha-LCAT activity on HDL is preserved.
Corneal opacification with fine stromal clouding (an 'arcus'-like haze) is near-universal and often the presenting feature in both forms.
Very low HDL cholesterol with a high proportion of unesterified plasma cholesterol is the biochemical signature.
Complete deficiency additionally causes normochromic haemolytic anaemia and progressive proteinuric renal disease that can advance to kidney failure.
Fish-eye disease is dominated by corneal clouding with low HDL but generally spares the kidneys and red cells.
Diagnosis combines lipid profiling, measurement of plasma LCAT activity and cholesterol esterification, and LCAT gene sequencing.
Management is largely supportive; the renal disease is the main determinant of long-term outcome and may recur after transplantation.
reference.pathophysiology: Lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase catalyses transfer of a fatty acid from phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) to free cholesterol, generating cholesteryl esters within circulating lipoproteins, chiefly HDL. This esterification is central to maturation of HDL particles and to reverse cholesterol transport, whereby peripheral cholesterol is returned to the liver. Biallelic loss-of-function LCAT variants abolish or reduce this activity, so plasma accumulates unesterified free cholesterol and abnormal lipoprotein species, including lipoprotein-X-like particles, while mature HDL fails to form and HDL cholesterol falls to very low levels. In complete (classic) deficiency both alpha activity on HDL and beta activity on apoB-containing particles are lost; in fish-eye disease residual alpha activity is absent but beta activity persists, producing a milder, largely ocular phenotype. Deposition of abnormal free-cholesterol-rich lipoproteins in the corneal stroma causes progressive opacification. In the kidney, these abnormal lipids accumulate in the glomerular basement membrane and mesangium, producing proteinuria, glomerular lipid deposits and progressive glomerulosclerosis. Incorporation of excess free cholesterol into erythrocyte membranes shortens red-cell survival, giving a target-cell-rich haemolytic anaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of very low HDL (Tangier disease, apolipoprotein A-I deficiency)
Cholestatic liver disease with lipoprotein-X and corneal changes
Other hereditary corneal dystrophies and stromal opacities
Alport syndrome and other hereditary glomerulopathies
additionalInvestigations: Fasting lipid profile with HDL cholesterol and ratio of free to esterified cholesterol
Plasma LCAT enzyme activity and cholesterol esterification rate
LCAT gene sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis
Slit-lamp corneal examination and ophthalmology assessment
Urinalysis, urine protein quantification and renal function tests
Full blood count and haemolysis screen with blood film for target cells
Renal biopsy with electron microscopy where nephropathy is suspected
redFlags: Progressive proteinuria or declining renal function indicating advancing nephropathy
Rapidly worsening corneal opacification affecting vision
Nephrotic-range protein loss with oedema and hypoalbuminaemia
Signs of established chronic kidney disease requiring renal replacement planning
reference.prognosis: Fish-eye disease usually follows a benign course limited to progressive corneal clouding, whereas complete deficiency carries a guarded prognosis owing to progressive renal disease that may reach kidney failure and can recur in a transplanted kidney.
pitfalls: Ascribing corneal clouding to ageing arcus and missing an underlying lipoprotein disorder
Interpreting very low HDL as laboratory error or secondary dyslipidaemia without considering LCAT deficiency
Overlooking early proteinuria that heralds serious renal involvement in complete deficiency
Assuming statins or standard lipid therapy will correct the metabolic defect
Failing to distinguish complete deficiency from fish-eye disease, which have very different renal risks
management: Manage supportively as no enzyme replacement is established in routine practice, using dietary fat restriction to limit abnormal lipoprotein-X formation
Provide nephroprotection for the progressive proteinuric renal disease with RAAS blockade, blood-pressure control and monitoring of proteinuria and renal function
Offer renal replacement therapy or transplantation for kidney failure, recognising the disease can recur in the graft
Manage the normochromic haemolytic anaemia, including transfusion when required
Undertake ophthalmological monitoring of corneal opacification, with corneal transplantation for visually significant clouding
Assess cardiovascular risk and individualise lipid management despite the characteristically very low HDL cholesterol
Provide genetic counselling with LCAT gene testing and family screening, given autosomal recessive inheritance
